title: Energy & Power
objective: Distinguish power from energy and understand energy density across primary fuels.

explanation.summary: Energy makes change possible. Power describes how quickly energy is transferred.
body: A lamp transfers electrical energy into light and heat. Its power tells you the rate; the energy used also depends on how long it stays on.
Chemical reactions rearrange electrons and bonds. Fission changes atomic nuclei, making nuclear fuel a concentrated source of energy.

details.title: Why does fuel energy density matter?
details.body: Energy per kilogram affects how much fuel must be mined, transported and stored. A comparison needs to say whether it counts raw material, prepared fuel or electricity actually delivered.

details.title: Where does the energy come from?
details.body: The mass difference between the initial particles and reaction products corresponds to released energy: ΔE = Δm × c². Much of the recoverable fission energy begins as motion of the fragments and becomes heat.

title: Inside the Atom
objective: Identify atomic structure, protons, neutrons, electrons, and isotopic stability.

explanation.summary: An atom has a small nucleus surrounded by electrons.
body: Protons carry positive charge, electrons carry negative charge, and neutrons have no electric charge. Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
The proton count identifies the element. Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are called isotopes.

details.title: What makes an isotope stable?
details.body: Nuclear stability depends on the balance of nuclear attraction and electrical repulsion, as well as the arrangement of protons and neutrons. A drawing of an atom cannot tell you its decay rate.

details.title: Why can heavy nuclei release energy?
details.body: Fission products can be more tightly bound per nucleon than the original heavy nucleus. The difference in total binding energy is released during the reaction.

title: Nuclear Fission
objective: Explain neutron-induced fission, chain reactions, and thermal neutron moderation.

explanation.summary: Fission splits a heavy nucleus, releasing energy and additional neutrons.
body: A captured neutron can lead to fission, but not every capture causes a split. The fragments transfer energy to their surroundings as heat.
Released neutrons may escape, be absorbed, or cause further fissions. A chain reaction continues when enough of them cause new splits.

details.title: Why slow neutrons down?
details.body: In light-water reactors, water acts as a moderator: collisions slow neutrons. The chance of fission depends on both the isotope and the neutron energy.

details.title: What does critical mean?
details.body: The effective multiplication factor, k_eff, compares neutron populations across generations. At k_eff = 1 the chain reaction is self-sustaining; below 1 it declines and above 1 it grows. Delayed neutrons affect how quickly it responds. This exhibit does not calculate k_eff.

title: The Nuclear Reactor
objective: Identify core reactor components including fuel assemblies, control rods, coolant, and pressure vessels.

explanation.summary: A reactor controls a chain reaction and carries the resulting heat away.
body: Fuel pellets are sealed inside metal tubes. Coolant carries heat from the fuel, while control rods absorb neutrons to regulate or stop the chain reaction.
In a pressurized water reactor, the primary coolant transfers heat through steam-generator tubes to a separate water circuit. That second circuit supplies steam to the turbine.

details.title: Why keep cooling after shutdown?
details.body: Stopping the chain reaction does not remove the heat produced by radioactive decay. Cooling remains necessary after shutdown.

details.title: What limits heat transfer?
details.body: Engineers evaluate temperatures, pressure and the transfer of heat through fuel and cladding into coolant. Limits and margins depend on the reactor design and operating conditions; this conceptual exhibit is not an operating simulator.

title: Generating Electricity
objective: Understand the thermal steam cycle, turbine-generators, and grid dispatchability.

explanation.summary: Steam turns a turbine, and the turbine drives an electrical generator.
body: A nuclear station converts heat into motion and then electricity. A condenser turns the turbine exhaust steam back into water for reuse.
Some heat must be rejected to the surroundings. Cooling arrangements may use rivers, seawater or cooling towers; they differ between plants.

details.title: Why is heat output larger than electric output?
details.body: A heat engine converts only part of its heat input into useful work. The temperature difference between the heat source and heat sink limits the possible efficiency. Actual plant performance also includes losses and the electricity used by equipment.

details.title: How does the steam cycle work?
details.body: The Rankine cycle describes heating and vaporizing water, expanding steam through a turbine, condensing it and pumping the liquid back. Reactor designs supply heat to this cycle in different ways.

title: Safety & Defense-in-Depth
objective: Examine defense-in-depth barrier architecture, passive safety systems, and historical accident lessons.

explanation.summary: Defense in depth combines barriers, cooling systems and operating practices.
body: Fuel, cladding, the coolant boundary and containment can help retain radioactive material. The exact barriers and backup systems depend on the design.
Safety also depends on maintenance, regulation, training and preparation for accidents. Multiple layers reduce risk; they do not make an accident impossible.

details.title: What does passive cooling mean?
details.body: Some systems use gravity, natural circulation or evaporation to move coolant and heat. Their capability still depends on conditions such as water inventory, available heat sinks and the duration of an event.

details.title: How is safety assessed?
details.body: Engineers examine accident sequences and the reliability of protective systems. Probabilistic assessments estimate risks under stated assumptions; historical experience and accident investigations provide a separate source of lessons.

title: Nuclear Waste & Byproducts
objective: Analyze radioactive decay, spent fuel cooling, dry cask containment, and deep geological repositories.

explanation.summary: Used nuclear fuel needs cooling, shielding and long-term management.
body: After leaving a reactor, spent fuel initially cools in a water pool. Suitable fuel can later move to engineered dry storage.
Different radioactive materials decay at different rates. Storage and disposal decisions must account for heat, radiation and the possibility of material reaching people or the environment.

details.title: Why is there no single waste lifetime?
details.body: Spent fuel is a mixture of isotopes. Some decay quickly and contribute much of the early heat; others persist for much longer. A half-life describes one isotope, not the time when an entire waste package becomes harmless.

details.title: How does geological disposal work?
details.body: Geological disposal combines a suitable site with engineered barriers to isolate waste over long periods. Reprocessing can recover usable material, but it also leaves waste requiring management; storage and permanent disposal are distinct tasks.
